pages.x: News of revolution in Paris and Vienna reached Pest in March 1848. On the 15th the young poet Sándor Petőfi read out his National Song to the crowds, with its call: Rise up, Hungarians! Students printed twelve demands without the censor's leave, and by evening the city was in the people's hands, without a shot fired.

In April the emperor accepted the April Laws, which gave Hungary its own government, ended serfdom and gave many more men the vote. The finance minister, Lajos Kossuth, a lawyer and a spellbinding speaker, became the voice of the revolution, and that autumn he toured the Great Plain raising volunteers for a new army, the Honvéd.

Vienna wanted its power back, and quietly encouraged Josip Jelačić, the ban of Croatia, whose people resented Hungarian rule, to invade. On 29 September 1848 the new Hungarian army stopped him at Pákozd, near Lake Velence, and he turned away toward Vienna. Hungary and the empire were now at war.

In December 1848 the 18-year-old Franz Joseph became emperor, and Prince Windischgrätz invaded Hungary with a large army. Pest fell in January 1849, and Kossuth's government fled east to Debrecen, behind the Tisza river. In the mountains to the north, General Artúr Görgei led his army on a daring winter march, and kept it alive.

In the spring of 1849 Görgei, a 31-year-old chemist turned general, struck back. His armies beat the Austrians at Isaszeg and in battle after battle, and by May they had driven them out of nearly all of Hungary and stormed Buda castle. In Transylvania the old Polish general Józef Bem won back the east.

On 14 April 1849, in the great Protestant church of Debrecen, the parliament declared Hungary independent and dethroned the House of Habsburg. Kossuth became governor-president. Soon after, Franz Joseph asked the tsar of Russia for help.

Tsar Nicholas I, who hated revolutions, sent about 200,000 soldiers over the Carpathians in June 1849, while a reinforced Austrian army attacked from the west. On 31 July Bem's army was routed at Segesvár, in Transylvania. Petőfi, who was with it, was last seen there, and his body was never found.

Caught between two empires, Kossuth handed power to Görgei and fled to the Ottoman Empire. On 13 August 1849, at Világos, Görgei laid down his arms with some 30,000 men, not to the Austrians but to the Russians. Many Hungarians called him a traitor, though he had no hope left.

Austria took its revenge. On 6 October 1849 thirteen Hungarian generals were hanged or shot at Arad, and the former prime minister, Batthyány, was shot in Pest. Hungarians say that because Austrian officers clinked their beer glasses to celebrate, they vowed not to clink beer for 150 years.
pages.of: Hungarian generals put to death at Arad

pages.x: The revolution failed, but not for nothing. Serfdom never came back, and in 1867 Franz Joseph made a deal with Hungary, the Compromise, which turned his empire into Austria-Hungary, with Hungary ruling itself. Kossuth died in exile in Turin, and 15 March is Hungary's national day.
pts: Hungary won its own government in 1848
Crushed by Austria and Russia in 1849
